1275.title: From soil to Om
1275.hook: the Chandogya follows a chain from the ground under your feet up to the chant, and finds Om at the end
1275.carry: om is the essence of all essences
1275.howItsDone: The Chandogya Upanishad, part of the Sama Veda's tradition, opens by teaching meditation on Om as the udgitha, the high chant, and is studied in Vedanta and recited in Vedic learning.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda: verses from the Rig Veda set to melody, opening with come, Agni, to the feast.
screen: `SAMAN: THE VERSE, SUNG.`

segments.voice: Orange juice in a carton. Before that, oranges in a crate. Before that, a tree; before that, rain and soil. Every glass at breakfast sits at the end of a chain nobody follows back. One old text follows a chain like that, link by link, from the ground up, but it isn't tracing breakfast. It's tracing a song. The Chandogya Upanishad belongs to the Sama Veda, and right at its start it asks what the very best part of everything is, and keeps going until it reaches the chant itself.
screen: `A GLASS OF JUICE, A CHAIN BEHIND IT.` → `ONE TEXT TRACES A SONG.` → `THE CHAIN THAT ENDS IN A CHANT.`

segments.voice: The Chandogya opens with the udgitha, the high chant, the part of a Sama Veda song the lead singer sends up. It says, in paraphrase: let a person meditate on the syllable Om as the udgitha, for the chant begins with Om. Then comes the chain. The essence of all beings is the earth. The essence of the earth is water. Of water, plants. Of plants, the human being. Of the human being, speech. Of speech, the Rig Veda's verses. Of the Rig Veda, the saman, the melody. And of the saman, the udgitha, which is Om. Each link is the rasa, the juice, the essence, of the one before. And the text crowns the last one: this, it says, is the essence of all essences, the highest. That's the teaching. For Hindus, Om isn't a warm-up noise in front of a prayer. It's the heart of all sacred sound. That's why Vedic recitation traditionally begins with Om, and why so many prayers and mantras in Hindu homes still open with it. And notice where the chain starts: with dirt. The Upanishad doesn't float the sacred syllable above ordinary things; it grows it from soil, water and food, through a body and a voice. So when a grandmother says Om before her prayer, many teachers would say she's starting at the heart of the whole chain, field and all.
screen: `THE UDGITHA: THE HIGH CHANT.` · `EARTH, WATER, PLANTS, PEOPLE, SPEECH.` · `VERSE, THEN MELODY, THEN OM.` · then, large: `OM: THE ESSENCE OF ALL ESSENCES.`

segments.voice: Sit tall. Feel the ground under you, then the water in you, then the last thing you ate, grown somewhere, then yourself here, walking the chain link by link. Then, as many Hindus do before a prayer, say Om slowly on the out-breath, three times if you like, letting it rise from the chest; if Om isn't yours, a quiet hum will do. Rest in the quiet after each one. If you pray, let your prayer begin from there.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, the melody is the essence of the verse, and Om, the heart of the chant, is the essence of all essences. Today's word.

1276.title: The breath the demons couldn't pierce
1276.hook: the gods and the demons were at war, and the gods reached for a song. the Chandogya tells which breath could carry it
1276.carry: prana: the breath evil couldn't pierce
1276.tomorrow: do the sounds between the words matter?
1276.howItsDone: The story of the gods, the demons and the breath is taught from the second section of the Chandogya Upanishad, part of the Sama Veda's tradition, where the high chant is meditated on as the main breath, prana.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: om is the essence of all essences. The Chandogya's chain ran from earth, water and food through voice and verse to the chant, and at its heart, Om.
screen: `FROM THE GROUND UP TO OM.`

segments.voice: The gods and the demons were at war. That's how the story starts, in the second section of the Chandogya Upanishad. And the gods decide their weapon will be a song. Not a spear, not a trick: the udgitha, the high chant. With this, they say, we'll overcome them. But a chant needs something to carry it, so the gods try one part of a person after another, and the demons follow them to each. Today: which breath can hold the song.
screen: `THE GODS AND THE DEMONS AT WAR.` → `THE GODS REACH FOR A SONG.` → `WHAT CAN CARRY IT?`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, it goes like this. First the gods sing the chant as the breath in the nose. The demons pierce it with evil, and that, the text says, is why we smell both the sweet and the foul. Next, speech. Pierced: that's why we speak both truth and falsehood. Then the eye, and we see both what's fitting and what isn't. Then the ear, and we hear both. Then the mind, and we think both kinds of thoughts. Each one cracks. Then the gods sing the chant as the breath in the mouth, the main breath, the one that keeps a body alive. The demons rush at it and scatter, the text says, the way a lump of earth flung at a solid rock breaks into pieces. Here's the teaching folded inside. Every sense in us is mixed; the same tongue blesses and lies. But underneath them is prana, the life-breath, going in and out on good days and bad, and in this story it's the one thing evil couldn't break. So the high chant is sung as prana: the song rides on the breath that keeps the singer alive. Hindu practice still puts the breath first. In sandhya, the daily prayers at dawn and dusk built around the Gayatri, a few rounds of pranayama, measured breathing, come before the mantra, and many formal pujas open the same way. Many teachers read this story as one old reason why: before you pray with a voice that can go either way, you begin from the breath that can't.
screen: `NOSE, SPEECH, EYE, EAR, MIND: PIERCED.` · `EACH ONE GOES BOTH WAYS.` · `THE MAIN BREATH: THE DEMONS SCATTER.` · `IN SANDHYA, THE BREATH COMES FIRST.` · then, large: `PRANA: THE BREATH EVIL COULDN'T PIERCE.`

segments.voice: Notice a smell in the room, a sound, a thought passing, each with its own mood. Then let them go and come to the breath: in slowly through the nose, a short easy pause, out slowly, the measured breath many Hindus take before sandhya or puja. Keep it gentle and never strain; if anything feels uncomfortable, just breathe normally. A few rounds, then rest in the plain breath. If you pray, let that breath carry your prayer.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, the high chant can't be carried by the senses or the mind. It's sung as the main breath, prana. Today's word.
screen: `THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: prana, the breath evil couldn't pierce. The song rides on it. See you tomorrow.

1277.title: This world is hau
1277.hook: na na na, hey hey. songs everywhere carry syllables that mean nothing. the Sama Veda's chants have them too, and the Chandogya gives them a world
1277.carry: upasana: seeing the whole world in the rite
1277.tomorrow: what does the song rest on?
1277.howItsDone: In Sama Veda chanting, the words of a verse are stretched and repeated and joined by syllables called stobhas, and the chants are learned from a teacher by ear.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, still in the Sama Veda: prana, the breath evil couldn't pierce. Every sense went both ways, and only the life-breath could carry the chant.
screen: `THE SONG RIDES ON THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Na na na na. Hey hey. Ooh, la la. Plenty of songs have a stretch where the words run out and the singer keeps going anyway. Nobody looks those syllables up. And yet a crowd of strangers will sing them back, louder than the verses. Sama Veda chant has syllables like that too, sounds slipped between the words of the verse to carry the melody. A reader could skip them as filler. The Chandogya Upanishad doesn't. Today: the sounds between the words.
screen: `NA NA NA. HEY HEY.` → `NOT IN ANY DICTIONARY.` → `THE SOUNDS BETWEEN THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: When a verse becomes a saman, a Sama Veda chant, the words don't stay as they were. Vowels stretch. Syllables repeat. And between them come extra sounds, with names like hau and hai and auhoyi. These are stobhas. On their own they don't mean anything the way a word does; they're there for the song. Then the Chandogya gives the stobhas the world. In paraphrase: this world is the sound hau. The wind is hai. The moon is atha. And it goes on down a list, pairing chant-sounds with fire, with the sun, with breath, with food. So the sounds a hurried listener would call filler, the Upanishad treats as the places where the whole world comes into the song. This is a way of worship the Upanishads teach again and again, called upasana, literally a sitting near: meditating on one part of a rite as something greater. The singer doesn't only sound hau; he holds this world in it. Readers take it more than one way. Some hear a meditation, a way to keep the whole world in mind while chanting. Some hear a point about sound itself: in Hindu practice a sacred sound can matter even where it carries no dictionary meaning, and Vedic chanters still learn every syllable by ear and keep it exact. Either way, the Chandogya refuses to throw the small sounds away. In this teaching, nothing in a rite is too small to hold the world.
screen: `STRETCHED, REPEATED, FILLED IN.` · `STOBHAS: HAU, HAI, AUHOYI.` · `THIS WORLD IS HAU. THE WIND IS HAI.` · then, large: `UPASANA: THE WHOLE WORLD IN A SMALL SOUND.`

segments.voice: On the out-breath let a soft open sound come, like haa or hau, quiet enough that no one else hears, just a sound with no meaning. On the next breaths make the same sound and let it hold one thing each time, the ground under you, the air in the room; if silence suits the place you're in, make the sound inside. If you pray, let it be prayer.

1278.title: What does the song rest on?
1278.hook: three singers sit down to talk shop, and one keeps asking: what holds that up? the answer goes all the way to space
1278.carry: the last ground of everything is brahman
1278.tomorrow: which Veda does Krishna call himself?
1278.howItsDone: The dialogue of Shilaka, Dalbhya and King Pravahana is taught from the Chandogya Upanishad, part of the Sama Veda's tradition, as a meditation on the high chant resting finally on space.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, still in the Sama Veda: upasana, seeing the whole world in the rite. The Chandogya hears this world, the wind and the moon in the chant's small sounds.
screen: `THE SOUNDS BETWEEN THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Why is the sky blue? Because of the light. Why? Because of the air. Why? Small children play this at bedtime, and the questions stop only when someone runs out of answers, or patience. The Chandogya Upanishad tells a story that runs like that. Three men skilled in the high chant of the Sama Veda sit down to talk about it, two brahmins and a king. And one question keeps getting asked, each time one step further down: what does that rest on?
screen: `WHY? BECAUSE. WHY?` → `THREE SINGERS SIT DOWN TOGETHER.` → `WHAT HOLDS UP A SONG?`

segments.voice: Their names are Shilaka, Dalbhya and Pravahana. Pravahana, the king, says: you two speak first; I'll listen. So Shilaka asks Dalbhya, in paraphrase: what does the saman, the chant, rest on? Dalbhya says: on tone, the sound of the voice. And tone? On breath. And breath? On food. And food? On water. And water? On that world, the heavens. And the heavens? Here Dalbhya stops. We don't lead the chant past the heavens, he says; we set it there. Shilaka isn't satisfied. The heavens, he says, rest on this world, the earth beneath us. Then Shilaka puts the question to the king: and this world, what does it rest on? Pravahana's answer: on space. All beings come out of space and go back into space, he says. Space is greater than all of them, the last support. Here the teaching opens wide. The Brahma Sutra, the classic summary of the Upanishads, stops at this very passage and asks: what is this space? Its answer, followed by Vedanta's great teachers, Shankara and Ramanuja among them: not empty air. It's Brahman, the one reality all beings come from and go back to, since only Brahman could be the source and end of everything. That's one of Hinduism's biggest ideas, arriving in a talk between three singers: under the song, the breath, the food and the earth, there is Brahman. A note only rings because there's room around it. In this teaching, everything rings in Brahman.
screen: `TWO BRAHMINS AND A KING.` · `TONE, BREATH, FOOD, WATER, HEAVEN.` · `AND THE EARTH? IT RESTS ON SPACE.` · `THE BRAHMA SUTRA: THAT SPACE IS BRAHMAN.` · then, large: `UNDER EVERYTHING, BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: At the end of each out-breath there's a small pause before the next breath comes; let your attention rest there without stretching it. Then listen for the quiet between one sound and the next, and the gap after a passing thought, the open room everything else happens in. If you pray, rest in prayer there.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, three singers ask what the chant rests on, all the way down to space, which Vedanta reads as Brahman. Today's word.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last ground of everything is Brahman. Three singers went down through breath, food and earth, until a king answered: space.

segments.voice: A book of songs. Indra, among the gods. The mind. Awareness. They share a single line of the Bhagavad Gita. This path has been in that chapter before, the tenth, where Krishna said, among meters, I am the Gayatri. Earlier in the same list, he names something this week has been listening to. After days of chants, breath and stobhas, it may not be a surprise what. Today, the last day on the Sama Veda: what Krishna says about it.

segments.voice: Arjuna has asked how he should think of Krishna, and Krishna answers with a list: in each kind of thing, one where he can be found. Among lights, the sun. Today's verse, Gita ten, twenty-two, begins: vedanam samavedo 'smi. Of the Vedas, I am the Sama Veda. Then, in the same breath: among the gods, I am Indra. Among the senses, the mind. In living beings, awareness. The Gita doesn't stop to explain why the Sama Veda; it says it and moves on. Some readers point to what we've seen these days. The Sama Veda is the Rig Veda's verses, sung: the words are the same, and what's added is melody. Remember the Chandogya's chain, where the essence of the verse is the chant. A verse sung is still the verse, but now it rings. Then Krishna gives the key to the whole list. In paraphrase: whatever is glorious, beautiful or mighty, know that it springs from a spark of my splendor. These are his vibhutis, the ways his glory shows through the world. That's a real Hindu way of seeing: God is behind everything, and shows most plainly where something shines. It's why a family may hear a fine singer's voice as Saraswati's gift, and why a well-sung chant can bring a grandmother to tears. Where should I look for you, Arjuna asked. One answer from this chapter: in whatever shines, and among the Vedas, in the one that is sung.

segments.voice: Close or soften your eyes and listen outward, traffic, a fan, a bird, a voice somewhere, the hum of a fridge, without naming anything. Then ask Arjuna's question gently, where should I look, and let your attention rest on whichever sound feels most like singing, or on your own breath if none does. If you pray, rest in prayer there.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Gita, Krishna says: of the Vedas, I am the Sama Veda, the Veda that is sung, one of his vibhutis. Today's word.

1280.title: Marrow to marrow
1280.hook: turmeric in warm milk at a sick child's bedside. one Veda turns from the great fire altar to rooms like that one
1280.carry: caring for the body is sacred: prayer with remedy
1280.howItsDone: The Atharva Veda holds hymns for healing fever, wounds and broken bones, often said together with a healing plant; its recitation is kept by Vedic chanters of its own schools.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-EIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the Sama Veda. Vibhuti: God shines through the best of each thing, and of the Vedas, Krishna said, I am the Sama Veda.

segments.voice: A saucepan on low heat. Milk, a spoon of turmeric, maybe a pinch of pepper, stirred until it goes gold. Then down the hall to a kid in bed with a cough and a warm forehead. In some homes that cup is a remedy handed down from grandparents. Nobody calls it scripture; it's just what you do when someone you love is sick. The Vedas we've read so far mostly stand at the great fire altar, with priests, hymns and melodies. The Atharva Veda walks down the hall, with hymns for fevers, wounds and broken bones. Today: the Veda of remedies.
screen: `TURMERIC IN WARM MILK.` → `DOWN THE HALL TO A SICK BED.` → `THE VEDA OF REMEDIES.`

segments.voice: The Atharva Veda's word for a remedy is bheshaja: medicine, cure, what makes well. It runs all through these hymns. Some are addressed to fever, some to plants, some to a wound or an aching limb. The healer speaks, the plant is given, and the hymn says what the healing should do. Listen to one, a hymn for setting a broken bone. In paraphrase: let marrow come together with marrow, joint with joint. Let what has fallen away of the flesh, and the bone too, grow back. It isn't abstract. It names the body part by part, the way a person setting a bone would have to think, and speaks a hope over each, that it knit. A plant goes with it: the hymn speaks to a healing herb and calls it rohani, the grower of the broken bone. So the hymn isn't a prayer floating above the injury. It's said right at the injury, while the bone is set and the herb is given. That's the turn the Atharva Veda makes. The Vedas this path has heard so far sing to the gods at the great rites. This one sits at the bedside too, and it's where Ayurveda, India's classical medicine, traces its roots: the old medical books call Ayurveda a limb of the Atharva Veda. So the teaching is plain. In Hinduism, caring for a body is sacred work, and prayer goes with the remedy, never instead of it. A grandmother who says a prayer over turmeric milk and then drives you to the doctor is standing in that line.
screen: `BHESHAJA: A REMEDY, A CURE.` · `MARROW TO MARROW, JOINT TO JOINT.` · `SAID AT THE INJURY, WITH THE HERB.` · `AYURVEDA: A LIMB OF THE ATHARVA VEDA.` · then, large: `PRAYER WITH THE REMEDY, NOT INSTEAD.`

If you pray, hold that place, or someone who is sick, in prayer.

1281.tomorrow: a hymn to the healer's own hands
1281.howItsDone: The Atharva Veda's hymns to takman, fever, address the sickness directly, naming its origin and its forms, offering it homage and asking it to depart; they belong to the Atharva Veda's healing hymns.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: caring for the body is sacred, prayer with the remedy. The bone hymn, marrow to marrow, joint to joint, said with the herb.

segments.voice: Homage to the cold fever. Homage to the burning one. Said aloud, it could be a line from a temple, offered to a god. It's said to a sickness. Anyone who has sat up at night beside someone burning and shivering may have muttered at the fever itself: go away, leave them alone. The Atharva Veda has hymns that speak to fever like that, as if it can hear. And one of them, before it asks the fever to leave, bows.
screen: `HOMAGE TO THE COLD FEVER.` → `SAID TO A SICKNESS.` → `THE HYMN THAT BOWS TO IT.`

segments.voice: The Atharva Veda's word for fever is takman, and in these hymns takman is spoken to like a someone, not a something. One hymn begins by naming where the fever comes from. In paraphrase: when fire entered the waters and burned, there, they say, is your birthplace. So the healer starts by knowing the fever's family: it came from fire. Then the hymn names its shapes. The cold fever. The burning one. The fever that comes back the next day, and the one that comes back on the third. Then the line from the start of today. Homage to the cold fever. Homage to the burning one. Namah: the same word people use to bow to a god, said to a sickness. Why bow first? The hymn doesn't explain. But the habit runs deep in Hinduism. The Shri Rudram, one of the most chanted Vedic hymns, opens with homage to Rudra's anger and to his arrow, and then asks him to be kind. Across north India, many families still honor Sheetala Mata, the cool one, a goddess linked with fevers and pox, praying that she'll be gentle with their children. One reading ties these together: Hindus bow even to the powers they fear. Name them fully, honor their strength, then ask them to pass gently. The bow isn't giving up. In the fever hymn, the homage comes with the request: leave. So the family at the bedside never pretends the sickness is small, and never stops asking it to go.
screen: `TAKMAN: FEVER, SPOKEN TO.` · `BORN WHERE FIRE ENTERED THE WATERS.` · `HOMAGE TO THE FEVER, THEN: GO.` · `THE RUDRAM: HOMAGE TO RUDRA'S ANGER.` · then, large: `BOW TO WHAT YOU FEAR. THEN ASK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time you were sick and someone stayed, a parent, a partner, a roommate, a nurse whose name you never learned, and see the room: the cloth, the glass of water, the voice in the dark. Let thanks rise toward them, whether they're near or far or gone, and if someone you know is sick now, hold them too, the way you were once held. If you pray, pray for them.
The Atharva Veda's healing hymns. Takman, fever: named by its birthplace and its shapes, given namah, homage, and asked to go. Today's word.
